task: Write one sentence of your own using the word frivolous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know frivolous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Aunt Rosa calls crossword puzzles a frivolous use of a sharp mind — then finishes ours in pen before the kettle boils.
A lighthearted joke suits the moment and harms nothing; frivolous goes further, spending real attention on what doesn't merit it.
Mindless sits past frivolous: a frivolous quiz at least amuses, while a mindless one asks nothing of you at all — no thought survives contact with it.

Trifling measures pure size: too small to deserve attention, whoever is paying it — a trifling sum, a trifling error. Frivolous measures a mismatch instead: something light claiming the time or money owed to weighty things. A trifling cost can be ignored; a frivolous purchase already spent the allowance.

Silly is the plain, everyday word for lacking sense — a silly answer just isn't reasonable. Frivolous makes a narrower charge: the thing may be perfectly sensible, only too light for the moment or the money it claims. A frivolous lawsuit can be argued with a straight face.
heavy with real stakes
grave in manner and purpose

Latin frivolus came into English whole and then kept to itself: apart from frivolity — the same word in noun form — the root built nothing else here. There is no cousin word to find; the word is its own small family.
Frivolous means of little importance.
With the levee story breaking, the night editor spiked the piece on a water-skiing poodle.
Nobody called the poodle boring — the newsroom had watched the clip nine times.
But page one belonged to the flood maps, and a frivolous item, however delightful, could wait for Sunday.
Frivolous doesn't mean bad or dull; it means light — of little importance — where weight is owed.
The poodle piece fails no test of fun, only the test of mattering.
That mismatch between lightness and the moment's seriousness is exactly what frivolous marks.
neutral, mildly disapproving
Frivolous judges a mismatch: light things given the time or money owed to weighty ones.
It is gentler than gratuitous — a unit-mate — which faults what nothing called for at all.
A frivolous purchase wastes an afternoon's allowance; a gratuitous insult has no excuse in the first place.

Every kilo on the sledge had to earn its place, so the expedition's packing list read like a sermon on necessity.
Fuel, pemmican, spare runners — and then, in Shackleton-era fashion, a banjo.
The committee back home called the instrument a frivolous indulgence: five kilos of varnished wood on a journey where men would shave grams off their spoons.
The captain overruled them.
Morale, he wrote, was not a luxury, and the banjo was cheap medicine for a dark winter.
Both sides, notice, agreed on the facts — the argument was over whether five kilos of music was weight stolen from survival or spent on it.
